commentary.bottom_line: Five studies suggest that repeating local validation after an update can detect performance loss that would otherwise go unnoticed and can confirm gains, but none compares sites that revalidate with sites that do not or measures patient outcomes. Hazard studies show that updates sometimes worsen local performance and sometimes improve it, so a site cannot predict the direction without checking.

perspectives.view: All five tests are retrospective replays, a pre-post series without a comparator, or automated benchmarks, and three are offline. Each reports accuracy or dosimetric metrics rather than patient outcomes, and none has a group that skipped revalidation. The findings point the same way, but design limits, indirectness, and small or single-site samples place certainty at very low.

After a software update kept the old cutoff, specificity fell from 45.8% to 23.1% and confirmatory testing rose 36.4%. Recalibrating to 0.480 restored specificity to 43.2% with 4.1% added testing. In radiotherapy, one update produced doses below a mandatory threshold, which led to a further iteration. Other studies report a threefold rise in recalls and specificity losses of 9% to 39%.

A deployed calibration check on 593,365 mammography studies verified that an updated model reached an AUC of 0.81 before acceptance. Control charts after a vendor segmentation upgrade showed four trend shifts and a moving average outside control limits for one structure while another improved. This suggests that structure-level monitoring may find changes that aggregate metrics hide. No study reports staff time or workflow burden.

One test in a cohort of 1,151,916 patients with a racial and ethnic minority focus found that refitting raised the C-index range from 0.69 to 0.84 to 0.79 to 0.85. A separate surgical study found that updates restored fairness in some cases and widened gaps in others. Subgroup results after an update may therefore need their own review.

Of 426 radiation oncology device recalls reported to the FDA from 2015 to 2025, software was the most common root cause at 45%, and 68 recalls involved AI-enabled devices. This suggests that vendor clearance and recall processes may not catch update problems before they reach sites, which supports local checks as a separate layer.

Several updates improved or did not change local performance, including contour agreement rising from 0.88 to 0.93 or higher and classifier utility rising from 81.1% to 84.1%. Many revalidations will therefore confirm acceptable performance. No study reports the cost or staffing needed, so a system may need to scale review effort to the size of each change.

On 33 pediatric tumor cases, a newer language model agreed with experts 57.6% of the time versus 77.1% for the prior version. Patients usually cannot see which version produced advice about them. Local checks after updates may be one of the few ways a health system learns that a tool has become less reliable.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems that revalidate after updates with those that do not on error rates reaching patients, clinical outcomes, or cost. Studies also do not define which kinds of updates warrant full revalidation versus lighter checks, or how much staff time each approach requires.
commentary.underserved_note: Tests of the practice included older adults in Viet Nam and a United States cohort with a racial and ethnic minority focus, but none enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether post-update performance changes differ in these groups, so local revalidation that reports subgroup results may be the only available source of that information.
